item.title: Marine Le Pen brought the far right to France’s front door
item.description:
Critics fist-bump on Paris streets after embezzlement conviction

PARIS (AP) — For years, Marine Le Pen stood at the gates of power, poised, relentless and rising. She stripped the French far right of its old symbols, sanded down its roughest edges and built in its place a sleek, disciplined machine with the single goal of winning the country’s presidency.

In 2022, she came closer than anyone thought possible, winning more than 40% of the vote in the runoff against Emmanuel Macron. The Elysee Palace seemed within reach.

Now her political future may lay in ruins. On Monday, a French court convicted Le Pen of embezzling European Union funds and barred her from holding office for five years. The sentence may have done more than potentially remove her from the next presidential race; it might have ended the most sustained far-right bid for power in Western Europe since World War II, surpassed only, in outcome, by Italy’s prime minister, Giorgia Meloni.

But the political earthquake Le Pen set in motion will rumble for years to come.

Le Pen was born in 1968 into a family already on the fringes of French politics. In 1972, her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, founded a National Front party rooted in racism, antisemitism and a yearning for France’s lost empire.

She was 8 years old when a bomb destroyed the family’s apartment in Paris in what was widely seen as an assassination attempt on her father. No one was seriously hurt, but the blast marked her for life. She has said it gave her a lasting sense that her family was hated and that they would never be treated like other people.

As a young woman, she studied law, became a defense attorney and learned how to argue her way through hostile rooms. In politics, she didn’t wait her turn. In 2011, she wrested control of the party from her father. In 2015, she expelled him after one of his Holocaust-denying tirades.

She renamed the party the National Rally. She replaced leather-jacketed radicals with tailored blazers and talking points. She talked less about race, more about the French way of life. She warned of “civilizational threats,” called for bans on headscarves and promised to put French families first.

Her tone changed. Her message didn’t.

In one of her sharpest political maneuvers, she sought out a group long despised by her father: the LGBTQ community. Le Pen filled her inner circle with openly gay aides, skipped public protests against same-sex marriage and framed herself as a protector of sexual minorities against “Islamist danger.”

Critics called it “pinkwashing,” a cosmetic tolerance masking deeper hostility. But it worked. A surprising number of gay voters, especially younger ones, started backing her. Many saw strength, clarity and the promise of order in a world spinning too fast.

She ran for president three times: 2012, 2017 and 2022. Each time, she climbed higher. In her final campaign, she was confident, calm and media savvy. She leaned into her role as a single mother, posed with her cats and repeated her calls for “national priority.” She no longer shocked. She convinced.

Behind her stood a constellation of far-right leaders cheering her on: Hungary’s Viktor Orban, Italy’s Matteo Salvini, the Netherlands’ Geert Wilders. They saw in her not only an ally but a leader. Her mix of cultural nationalism, social media fluency and calculated restraint became a blueprint.

“Marine Le Pen posts pictures of her cat, talks about being a mother. But when it comes to policy, there’s no softening,” said Pierre Lefevre, a Paris-based consultant. “It makes extreme positions seem more palatable, even to people who might otherwise be put off.”

When she lost in 2022, she didn’t vanish. She regrouped, stayed present in parliament and prepared for 2027. Polls had her leading. Macron cannot run again.

Then came Monday’s verdict.

The court found Le Pen had siphoned millions of euros in public funds while serving in the European Parliament, paying party staff with money intended for EU assistants. Prosecutors described it as deliberate and organized; the court agreed.

She was sentenced to two years of house arrest, fined 100,000 euros ($108,200) and banned from holding public office for five years. She said she would appeal. The house arrest sentence will be suspended during the appeal, but the ban on holding office takes effect immediately.

Her allies erupted in outrage. Orban declared, “Je suis Marine” — I am Marine. Salvini called the ruling “a declaration of war by Brussels.” In Paris, her supporters called it political persecution; her opponents fist-pumped in the streets.

Even in disgrace, Le Pen remains one of the most consequential political figures of her time. She took a name that once evoked hatred and transformed it into a serious vehicle for national leadership. She made the far right electable. She blurred the line between fringe and power.

Her party, the National Rally, became the largest last year in France’s lower house of parliament. Her handpicked successor, 29-year-old Jordan Bardella, now leads it. He is polished and popular but lacks broad political experience and name recognition.

Whether Le Pen returns after her ban, fades into silence or again reinvents herself, her mark is permanent. She forced mainstream rivals to adapt to her language. She turned fear into votes and redefined what was politically possible in a republic once seen as immune to extremism.

She never became president, but she changed the race and the rules.

item.title: BOJ quarterly survey signals decline in Japan business mood
item.description:
Tankan assessment comes as Trump tariffs roil global trade

TOKYO — Business sentiment among large Japanese manufacturers declined slightly in the first three months of the year, the Bank of Japan’s latest Tankan survey showed on Tuesday.

The headline diffusion index (DI) was at plus 12 for the period, compared with plus 14 in the previous quarter. The median forecast in a QUICK survey of economists was plus 12.

The data comes as sluggish domestic consumption and a slowdown in overseas demand overshadow Asia’s second-largest economy, with rising concern over U.S. President Donald Trump’s threats to impose tariffs also stoking uncertainty. The American leader last week announced a 25% levy on imported autos and car parts.

The closely-watched survey is considered one of the key indicators on the state of the Japanese economy and can be a major influence on the central bank’s monetary policy decisions. The DI is calculated by subtracting the percentage of companies that have pessimistic business sentiment from those that are optimistic.

Among large nonmanufacturers, the index was plus 35, compared with plus 33 in the October-December quarter.

item.title: Intel is still committed to foundry business, new CEO says
item.description:
Lip-Bu Tan said he will work closely with Trump White House to rebuild American chip giant

PALO ALTO, California — American chip giant Intel’s new CEO said the company is still committed to building a foundry business despite recent setbacks and is on track to begin mass production using its proprietary 1.8-nanometer chipmaking technology in the second half of the year.

“Our ambition is ultimately to create the best products and become the best foundry over the years,” Lip-Bu Tan said in a keynote speech at Intel Vision on Monday afternoon.

Tan, a semiconductor industry veteran, was named as Intel’s new CEO on March 12, three months after the December surprise announcement of predecessor Pat Gelsinger’s retirement.

Gelsinger left Intel with a bleeding balance sheet, unfinished massive production facilities and a foundry business at a crossroads. There have been reports of Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. proposing to take over Intel’s contract chipmaking business through a joint venture with partners including Broadcom and Nvidia. But Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang this month denied any involvement in such negotiations.

“Global demand for chip production is growing, and you need supply chains that are flexible, resilient and secure,” Tan said at Monday’s event. “Intel foundry plays a crucial role.”

“We will continue to advance our foundry strategy to meet our needs,” he said.

Intel has lagged behind top two contract manufacturers TSMC and South Korea’s Samsung Electronics in terms of how many transistors they can squeeze onto a single chip.

Tan said the company will continue working on its 18A and 14A chipmaking technologies, with mass production using 18A to begin in the second half as the company needs to use it to manufacture its in-house next-generation Panther Lake processors.

“We are the only American company that designs and manufactures advanced chips — that means that we have an essential role,” Tan said, adding that he is looking forward to working closely with the Trump administration and will ask for Washington’s help to “do what we need to do.”

In November, the U.S. Department of Commerce finalized up to $7.86 billion funding for Intel under the CHIPS and Science Act. This should provide some relief to Intel, which has struggled to keep up with the $100 billion investment commitment it made to its foundry business amid revenue declines.

But U.S. President Donald Trump has injected uncertainty into Intel’s plans, calling for scrapping the act and using undisbursed funds to reduce government debt.

All major CHIPS and Science Act grant terms were finalized in the last few months of the Biden administration. But the majority of the funds will not be disbursed until the chipmakers hit certain milestones for their U.S. fabs.

Meanwhile, Intel has fallen behind rivals Nvidia and AMD in capturing the artificial intelligence tailwind, with sales of both edge and data center AI chips tumbling.

“In the broader AI data area, I’m not happy with our current position,” Tan said Monday. Recruiting top talent in the industry will be a priority for the company as it works on more competitive chips for clients, he said.

Before Intel, Tan served as the CEO of chip design software company Cadence Design Systems from 2009 to 2021. The Malaysian-born, Singapore-raised industry veteran started his career in Silicon Valley as a venture capitalist in the 1980s.

Intel shares have dropped 49% in the past 12 months. They were down around 1% in extended trading after Tan’s speech.

item.title: Japan’s GPIF sticks to even bond-stock mix for next five years
item.description:
Pension whale sees rising interest rates improving bond performance

TOKYO — Japan’s Government Pension Investment Fund said Monday that it will continue aiming for bonds to make up around half of its portfolio over the next five years, counting on rising interest rates to lift returns.

Under its new medium-term plan starting in fiscal 2025, the GPIF, one of the world’s largest institutional investors, will maintain a four-way split of 25% each in domestic stocks, foreign stocks, domestic bonds and foreign bonds.

At the same time, it will raise its target for real investment return to 1.9% from 1.7%.

The GPIF’s decision comes as interest rates climb worldwide, boosting expected rates of return for bonds. Bonds are also considered less risky than stocks, making them especially attractive amid uncertainty over the global economy.

Still, the GPIF saw a need for a certain level of stockholdings. As wages rise, expected returns for the pension fund also rise, making it necessary to incorporate a proportionate amount of stocks highly correlated with wage growth.

“There were incentives to increase both stocks and bonds, resulting in a tug of war,” GPIF President Masataka Miyazono told a news conference Monday. “Through a multifaceted risk analysis, we were able to confirm that the goal can be achieved with an asset composition of 25% each,” he said.

Also on Monday, the GPIF released a summary of discussions regarding its new medium-term plan.

One attendee apparently had cited rising stock prices and a weak yen as major contributors to the fund’s recent performance but warned of a “high possibility of downward pressure” in the future.

The summary also demonstrated the difficulty of altering the makeup of the GPIF’s 258.7 trillion yen ($1.72 trillion) in managed assets as of December.

“Changing the composition by 5 percentage points would require asset transactions of more than 10 trillion yen in one direction alone,” said an attendee, who suggested maintaining the status quo.

item.title: Tokyo Gas to buy Texas shale stake from Chevron
item.description:
Deal expected in April as Japanese utility turns to natural gas trading

TOKYO — Tokyo Gas has decided to acquire part of a shale gas development in Texas from U.S. oil major Chevron, Nikkei has learned, as the Japanese energy company looks to expand profit through trading.

The deal, estimated at tens of billions of yen (10 billion yen equals $66.6 million), is expected as early as April. Tokyo Gas will use the natural gas it extracts from the development to trade on the market, as well as supply the fuel to power plants and other customers.

Because natural gas produces about half the carbon dioxide at fossil fuel plants compared with coal, Tokyo Gas anticipates that demand will continue to rise. The enthusiasm for shale gas expressed by U.S. President Donald Trump also was a factor.

At the end of 2023, Tokyo Gas bought Rockcliff Energy, a Texas-based shale gas developer, for around 400 billion yen. The Japanese utility will acquire a new interest close to Rockcliff and reduce the costs of laying pipeline to transport shale gas.

Tokyo Gas is in the process of replacing inefficient assets. In February, the company reached a basic agreement to sell its stake in a shale gas development in southern Texas to Shizuoka Gas for around 20 billion yen.

Tokyo Gas handles about 10 million tonnes of natural gas yearly in the U.S. in terms of liquefied natural gas volume. The Chevron deal will maintain this scale.

The Japanese company’s shale operations averaged an annual operating profit of about 13.5 billion yen from fiscal 2020 to fiscal 2024. Tokyo Gas aims to lift this annual profit to nearly 70 billion yen from fiscal 2025 to fiscal 2030. It plans to invest almost 300 billion yen in its shale business over the three years through fiscal 2028.

By concentrating shale investments in the Haynesville formation, which stretches from Texas to Louisiana, Tokyo Gas hopes to boost production while keeping costs down. Last year, the utility took a 49% stake in the trading subsidiary of major North American natural gas marketing firm ARM Energy Holdings, providing a channel of its own for selling the gas that it extracts.

item.title: Japan’s Brother eyes machine tool markets in Southeast Asia, Europe
item.description:
President Kazufumi Ikeda weighs M&A and tie-ups to meet customer needs

NAGOYA, Japan — Japanese printer maker Brother Industries sees Southeast Asia and Europe as the key to growing its machine tool business under its medium-term plan through 2028, with more manufacturers shifting away from China amid its rivalry with the U.S., President Kazufumi Ikeda told Nikkei.

Edited excerpts from the interview follow.

Q: What is your goal in strengthening your machine tool business in Southeast Asia and Europe?

A: In China, as tensions with the U.S. heighten, we’re seeing automakers and other manufacturers move production facilities to Southeast Asia. Electric vehicles are on the rise in Southeast Asia, and we also expect demand in areas outside the automotive industry in the future. We already have a sales office in Thailand, and we plan to add more staff and offices going forward.

China currently accounts for much of our machine tool sales. We want to build up in other regions to reduce our reliance on it.

Europe has a lot of high-mix, low-volume manufacturers that make parts for a variety of industries, such as aviation, health care and semiconductors. We previously focused on general-purpose equipment, which didn’t let us fully tap into this market.

Now, we have a lineup of high-performance products, such as multitasking machines. The 100-tool machine that we recently developed was made with European customers that want to improve productivity in mind.

Brother Industries recently developed a machine tool aimed at European manufacturers seeking to boost productivity. (Brother)

Q: You aim to double sales in your industrial equipment business in three years to 100 billion yen ($670 million).

A: If we can achieve that, operating profit of 15 billion yen will be within reach. But we can’t grow our sales by just marketing the compact, affordable products where our strengths lie. We’re looking at mergers and acquisitions as well as partnerships as ways to increase our scale without relying on market conditions.

We need knowledgeable talent that can understand what kind of processing our customers want to do and offer all-in-one proposals including automation before and after. Though we’re internally training and externally hiring key sales staff who are also engineers, it’s time-consuming. We want to partner with outside manufacturers and systems integrators that already have strengths in this.

Q: You’ve also positioned industrial printing as a growth area. What opportunities do you see there?

A: In the U.S., our main market for garment printers, there’s a strong need for automation with labor costs rising. We’ll make suggestions such as bundling our printers with automated lines. We’ll also pair them with our label printer used for packaging.

Our printer heads eject ink with a lot of force, so they can handle high-viscosity industrial ink. We’ll move forward with technical innovations to improve resolution and yield while reducing costs to enhance our competitiveness.

item.title: U.S. hits Hong Kong officials with sanctions for ‘transnational repression’
item.description:
Justice secretary and five others targeted for undermining freedoms in city and beyond

NEW YORK — The U.S. on Monday announced sanctions targeting Hong Kong Justice Secretary Paul Lam as well as five other Hong Kongers and mainland Chinese who have played a role in eroding Hong Kong’s freedoms and in connection with acts of what Washington calls “transnational repression.”

The State Department designated Lam; Sonny Au, secretary-general for the Committee for Safeguarding National Security of the Hong Kong Special Administrative Region; and Dong Jingwei, director of China’s national security office overseeing Hong Kong. The other three targets are Police Commissioner Raymond Siu and two assistant commissioners of the national security police: Dick Chung Chun Wong and Margaret Chiu.

“Beijing and Hong Kong officials have used Hong Kong national security laws extraterritorially to intimidate, silence, and harass 19 pro-democracy activists who were forced to flee overseas, including a U.S. citizen and four other U.S. residents,” the State Department said in a fact sheet.

Rights groups and Hong Kong, Uyghur and Tibetan dissidents have raised concerns over the Chinese government’s efforts to repress or silence overseas activism through coercive measures including harassment of family members in China and even surveillance on U.S. soil.

Other incidents of alleged transnational repression include anonymous letters sent in Australia, offering a reward for information on the whereabouts of Australian citizen and Hong Kong democracy activist Kevin Yam.

The State Department said the sanctions, which will block their assets in the U.S. and prohibit any transactions with Americans, came in response to extraterritorial efforts by Beijing to silence an American citizen and four other U.S. residents.

Joey Siu, a U.S. citizen who moved from Hong Kong at a young age, previously told Nikkei Asia that she had been a victim of transnational repression while in the U.S., with Chinese authorities having put a 1 million Hong Kong dollar ($128,560 at current rates) bounty on her head in 2023 for her arrest on charges that she violated the security law.

Siu told Nikkei Asia on Monday that the latest sanctions are long overdue and that she is “delighted” to see action finally be taken.

“This really sends a strong signal to both Beijing and Hong Kong authorities that their act of transnational repression on American soil [and] beyond, on the soil of democracies, will be held accountable,” she said.

Siu expressed hope that the Trump administration will invest in law enforcement resources for those at risk of, or already subject to, transnational harassment.

The Hong Kong government strongly condemned the sanctions and said in a news release that it will not be intimidated by Washington’s “despicable behaviour” and will continue to pursue those it suspects of endangering national security.

“The specified absconders mentioned in the US statement are wanted and have arrest warrants issued by the court against them not because they ‘exercised their freedom of speech’, but because they have been at large in the US, the United Kingdom (UK) and Australia, etc. and continue to blatantly engage in activities endangering national security, including inciting secession and requesting foreign countries to impose ‘sanctions’ or blockade and engage in other hostile activities against the People’s Republic of China and the HKSAR,” a Hong Kong government spokesman said in the release.

The Biden administration announced sanctions on Hong Kong Chief Executive John Lee and 10 others in August 2020, about a month after a sweeping national security law imposed on Hong Kong by mainland China took effect. The U.S. said they had undermined the city’s autonomy and restricted freedom of expression or assembly there.

Hong Kong, a former British colony, was returned to Chinese rule in 1997 with a promise of 50 years of freedom of expression and assembly that were not enjoyed on the mainland.

Human rights groups and activists have condemned the Chinese government for undermining the rule of law and locking up hundreds of political prisoners, including tycoon Jimmy Lai, a staunch supporter of the pro-democracy movement.

The U.S. has provided Hong Kongers who have fled the city with a temporary legal status that allows them to remain in the country. The Deferred Enforced Departure program was extended for 24 months under a measure announced in January by Joe Biden, days before he stepped down as president to make way for Donald Trump.

item.title: Without a coup, Pakistan’s military has grabbed permanent rule
item.description:
Nation's armed forces now control the economy, judiciary and governance

Salman Rafi Sheikh is assistant professor of politics at the Mushtaq Ahmad Gurmani School of Humanities and Social Sciences at Lahore University of Management Sciences.

In 2024, Pakistan’s security forces conducted 59,775 intelligence-based operations targeting Islamist militants and Baloch separatists. More than anything else, the scale of these operations not only indicates the military’s control of national security but also its capability to impose a military solution on issues that could be resolved through political means or by strengthening civilian institutions, such as the Counterterrorism Department.

This pattern is a direct result of the military’s sustained political dominance in Pakistan over several decades. More recently, this ascendancy has reached unprecedented levels, largely due to the military’s manipulation of electoral processes to ensure civilian governments remain dependent on the military for survival.

Unlike previous military coups, which saw brief stints of direct military rule, the military’s role in Pakistan today is legally institutionalized, both politically and economically. At the helm of this legalization is not a military dictator but an elected civilian government. A clear example of this pattern of militarized governance is the Special Investment Facilitation Council (SIFC). Established in June 2023 via a parliamentary act, the SIFC includes several high-ranking and serving military officials, including the chief of the army staff (COAS), and serves as a “single window” for securing international investments and overseeing domestic economic projects. Importantly, it enjoys broad immunity, protecting its members from legal scrutiny and accountability.

The SIFC’s activities provide a much deeper glimpse into the military’s expanding political and economic footprint. In February 2024, Pakistan’s chief justice called for the federal government to ensure that the military’s focus remained strictly on defense matters — a reference to the military’s multibillion-dollar business empire being run via 50 commercial companies. The army also owns Pakistan’s largest housing society. The SIFC also blatantly proceeded to allocate 4.8 million acres of land for military-run corporate farming as part of the Green Pakistan Initiative in August 2024, signaling further military entrenchment in Pakistan’s political economy.

Pakistani soldiers are pictured on a tank during the Pakistan Day military parade in Islamabad on March 23, 2022.   © Reuters

More importantly, this expanding influence comes at the expense of established constitutional bodies and Pakistan’s federal structure. For instance, while the Council of Common Interests (CCI) — responsible for decisions on joint federal-provincial matters — has not convened even once since the current government took office after the controversial general election in 2024, the SIFC has met on at least 10 occasions. One of its decisions, which otherwise requires the CCI’s consent, was the construction of six new canals on Pakistan’s rivers to support military-run corporate farming.

This pattern of bypassing civilian institutions underscores the military’s growing (and legally entrenched) political and economic influence. In 2023, Pakistan’s parliament amended the Army Act, formalizing the military’s role in administering state functions and creating space for institutions like the SIFC, as well as for the appointment of retired military officials to civilian posts.

To make sure that these laws and institutions are permanently protected, the military-backed regime passed the 26th constitutional amendment in 2024 to ensure the judiciary’s subordination. Among other things, a key change involves the procedure for appointing the chief justice of the Supreme Court. Before the amendment, the senior-most judge of the Supreme Court would become the chief.

A parliamentary commission is now authorized to select the chief justice from among the three most senior judges. Dominated by the ruling coalition, which relies on military support, this system of so-called parliamentary oversight ensures that the chosen judge prioritizes the regime’s and the military interests. Unsurprisingly, after the new chief justice was appointed under this procedure, the Supreme Court ruled in late 2024 that the military could not only operate military courts but could also conduct civilian trials — effectively establishing a parallel judicial system.

At the same time, the military’s expansion has been criticized. Instead of reforming itself as a professional force, the military’s response has been to both criminalize dissent and normalize military domination.

Criminalization of dissent, putting severe limits on freedom of expression, has taken place via recent changes to the Prevention of Electronic Crimes Act. Still, army top brass have been touring universities to “engage” with the youth, Pakistan’s largest demographic group. Being privy to the details of one such tour allows me to describe them as an effort by the military to propagate notions of the militarization of politics as the new normal in Pakistan — i.e., something that is legal and must not be challenged.

This new normal, however, is not a coincidence. In many ways, it is due to Pakistan’s structurally and politically weak political parties and their perpetual tendency to rely on the military for winning political power.

The price that Pakistan is paying for this fatal mistake is permanent military rule. Unless civilians decide to build and use an alternative, such as genuinely electoral paths to power, the military is here to stay. This keeps Pakistan’s governance undemocratic to its core.

item.title: Japan’s young politicians lack power, leaving talent wasted: expert
item.description:
Japan Foresight founder urges debate on what country's democracy should look like

TOKYO — Roughly three decades since Japanese electoral reform that ushered in single-seat districts, the country still lacks a political system that allows young politicians to attain positions of power, according to Tobias Harris, founder of political consultancy firm Japan Foresight.

A sense of looking to the future is missing in Japanese politics, Harris told Nikkei in a recent interview.

Edited excerpts from the interview follow.

Q: How do you see the dissatisfaction among Japanese voters?

A: I think there’s just this feeling of it’s the same people over and over again. There’s not new people, there’s not new voices. Maybe that’s just another avenue of reform.

In some other democracies, you have seen more of an ability for young people to move to positions of authority sooner, and that could at least create a sense of responsiveness to the voices of younger people who are maybe not well represented — just a sense of change, a sense of looking towards the future. And that’s important.

I feel like that’s missing [in Japan]. I feel like maybe the public is responding to that.

The [ruling Liberal Democratic Party] manages to attract new candidates, many younger candidates, who may be coming from business or international organizations. But then they get elected, and they’re stuck in the seniority system, and they can’t do anything. They have no real power. They just have to sort of wait their turn and win elections. And then, maybe gradually they feel like they have more power. But there’s a sense of talent being squandered.

Q: What sort of political reforms do you believe Japan needs?

A: Probably the discussion that needs to happen is looking at the Heisei [1990s] reform, looking at this process of building a strong executive and saying we’ve built the strong executive, but it seems that there isn’t enough accountability. There aren’t enough checks on its power. Is there a way of making the Diet more capable of holding the government accountable?

Also, electorally speaking, is this mix of single-member districts and proportional representation producing the best kind of mix? Do we need to go either much more proportional or much more of a plurality system, and move closer to an approximation of a two-party system?

You are stuck in this situation where you do have the LDP, and then you have all these other parties that struggle to unify, and the proportional system keeps too many parties around, so how do you decide which direction you want go?

Q: What is missing from the discussion compared with the electoral reforms debate three decades ago.

A: You look back on the earlier reforms, there was a clear philosophy they were aiming for. And it was made very clear, right? The goal is a more decisive government, a more top-down government.

What should Japanese democracy look like? How do we want it, how does it differ from where we are now, and how do we get there? Maybe this debate is still at a very early stage. It’s going to take time to think through this and sort out what the right answer is to these questions.

Q: Social media is having a larger influence on elections. What response do you think is needed to address this?

A: It can be tremendously powerful. Obviously, the ability to deliver your message directly to voters really can be potent, particularly when you have populist appeals — they go great when you’re appealing directly to vote. That is understandable, but of course, the speed with which lies, deliberate misinformation and accidental [misinformation] can be amplified and spread is tremendously dangerous.

Japan maybe has the advantage that it’s a little behind the curve in the role of social media politics, and it has the opportunity to learn from other democracies and how they’ve perhaps been undone by social media.

item.title: U.S. bolsters ‘second island chain’ defense with eye on China
item.description:
Investment on Pacific island reflects threat of Beijing's growing missile capabilities

WASHINGTON — On his first trip to the Indo-Pacific as U.S. defense secretary last week, Pete Hegseth embraced America’s alliances and reaffirmed its commitment to sustaining robust deterrence in the region, including across the Taiwan Strait.

But he also made a little-noticed announcement at the start of the trip that points to another priority for the second Trump administration’s Indo-Pacific strategy: bolstering the “second island chain.”

Hegseth and Wesley Simina, president of the Federated States of Micronesia, announced on March 27 that the U.S. will begin planning and constructing key infrastructure projects in the state of Yap, roughly 850 kilometers from Guam.

Future investments in Micronesia and Yap by the U.S. Department of Defense are estimated to exceed $2 billion, the announcement said. “These projects are designed to provide strategic operational and exercise capabilities for U.S. forces,” it explained.

The investment reflects the rising importance of the second island chain, experts told Nikkei Asia. The chain covers a stretch of islands from Japan to Guam and the islands of Micronesia. They are farther from China than the “first island chain” — which comprises the Kuril Islands, the main Japanese archipelago, Okinawa, Taiwan and the northern part of the Philippine archipelago — which is more vulnerable to China’s rising missile threat.

Yap is one of the four states that constitute the Federated States of Micronesia. Under the Compacts of Free Association agreements with Micronesia, Palau and the Marshall Islands, the U.S. enjoys exclusive access to the land, sea and air routes of these island nations.

The announcement did not break down the investments. But the U.S. and Micronesia have been discussing — since the early years of the Biden administration — airfield modernization and seaport upgrades in Yap, commercial port improvements in Kosrae, the construction of a pre-engineered warehouse in Pohnpei, and basic harbor infrastructure enhancements in Chuuk.

The U.S. maintains a dominant security presence in the Southwest Pacific, with air and naval bases in Guam, a ballistic missile defense test site in the Marshall Islands, and a high-frequency radar system being built in Palau. The airport upgrade and expected deployment of air defense assets in Yap add to this position of strength.

Alessio Patalano, professor of war and strategy in East Asia at Kings College London, told Nikkei Asia that the U.S. has been systematically transforming its presence across the Indo-Pacific “to enhance versatility and mobility” and that the announcement in Micronesia sits within this reconfiguration.

The transformation reflects “an appreciation of the highly contested nature of the air dimension of the region’s battlespace,” said Patalano, who pointed to China’s increasing missile reach and the exposed nature of U.S. bases within the first island chain.

In a Stimson Center report published in December, analysts Kelly Grieco and Hunter Slingbaum as well as Air Force Lt. Col. Jonathan Walker noted that missile attacks by the People’s Liberation Army Rocket Force could close the runways and taxiways at U.S. forward air bases in the critical first days, and even weeks, of a Sino-American war.

“These attacks would prevent the U.S. Air Force from conducting fighter operations for about the first 12 days of a conflict from U.S. air bases in Japan,” they added.

Patalano said the investments in Yap suggest that the Trump administration is focusing on a “strategy of denial” as its baseline for deterrence, rather than one of dominance within the East China Sea or the Taiwan Strait.

“This in turn is compatible with an assumption that U.S. support to allies within the first island chain should not be taken for granted, and that the U.S. will ask more of them to ensure its continued presence,” he said.

A strategy of denial — advocated by U.S. President Donald Trump’s nominee for undersecretary of defense for policy, Elbridge Colby, calls for the U.S. and allies to find ways to deny China the ability to dominate the Indo-Pacific without having to defeat Beijing outright.

But Stimson’s Grieco told Nikkei Asia that while the focus on the second island chain makes a lot of sense, she does not see it as deprioritizing the first island chain.

“The second island chain is actually really important to the defense of the first island chain because China has fewer missiles that can reach the second island chain and those missiles are more expensive,” she said.

“Every time you have an additional location in the second island chain, it would mean that China would have to have more locations they need to strike, which thins out their missile salvos,” Grieco said.

Mira Rapp-Hooper, a former National Security Council senior director for East Asia and Oceania in the Biden administration, told Nikkei that the Yap infrastructure investment is a project the Biden administration had been pursuing for years.

“PLA objectives are to push out to and past the second island chain, so we need to solidify our own positions as well as those of our partners,” she said.

item.title: TSMC touts new 2-nm Taiwan chip fab, seeking balance with U.S. plans
item.description:
With $45bn plant, chipmaker hopes to allay public worries about local industry

TAIPEI — Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. on Monday held a ceremony for the upcoming launch of a next-generation fabrication facility in Kaohsiung, signaling its commitment to developing and producing state-of-the-art chips in Taiwan even amid big investments in the U.S.

“We will continue to expand investment in Taiwan in close consultation with the relevant agencies,” Y.P. Chyn, TSMC’s co-chief operating officer, said at the event for the facility, in which the chipmaker is investing more than 1.5 trillion New Taiwan dollars ($45.2 billion).

Taiwanese Premier Cho Jung-tai also stressed that “TSMC’s plan to expand globally while setting its roots in Taiwan has not changed.”

TSMC controls over 60% of the global semiconductor foundry market, with yields and performance outstripping those of rivals Intel and Samsung Electronics. The company holds a near-monopoly on production of artificial intelligence chips designed by Nvidia.

The Taiwanese chipmaker plans to start mass production of cutting-edge 2-nanometer chips in Taiwan in the second half of this year starting at a new facility in Hsinchu, followed by the new Kaohsiung plant. This will be two to three years ahead of the planned start of 2-nm production at TSMC’s second Arizona fab.

Equipment for mass production is being installed and set up at the first fab at the new Kaohsiung facility, while two more fabs remain under construction. Holding the ceremony now, with full-scale production still some way off, appears intended to allay worries in Taiwan about TSMC’s growing investment in the U.S.

Y.P. Chyn, TSMC’s co-chief operating officer, spoke at a ceremony for the company’s new Kaohsiung fab on March 31. (TSMC)

CEO C.C. Wei in March said TSMC would invest another $100 billion in the U.S., with three more advanced fabs to be built there alongside the three already announced.

U.S. President Trump has long complained that Taiwan “stole” chip business from the U.S., and TSMC’s March announcement has not resolved that tension, with the risk of additional chip tariffs ongoing.

The Trump administration has reportedly requested that TSMC help run Intel’s foundry business, with the Taiwanese company said to have approached multiple U.S. chip companies about investing in a joint venture overseeing the business.

In Taiwan, there are deep public concerns about TSMC’s U.S. investments leading to technology leaks or hollowing out the industry at home. Though the ruling Democratic Progressive Party has emphasized supply chain cooperation in the U.S., it looks to keep advanced technology that is crucial to economic security within Taiwan.

For TSMC, its investments in the U.S. and Taiwan serve different goals. Around 70% of the chipmaker’s sales are to North American customers, and investing in the U.S. allows it to work more closely with U.S. tech giants that are competitive in AI, such as Nvidia.

Taiwan, meanwhile, offers the advantage of a strong supply chain. In addition to the industry hub in Hsinchu, where TSMC is based, southern Taiwan — including Kaohsiung — has in recent years attracted more suppliers, including foreign players.

“The mature industry ecosystem can’t be replicated outside Taiwan,” said Liu Pei-chen at the Taiwan Institute of Economic Research, a private-sector think tank, citing benefits such as around-the-clock support for production facilities. Taiwanese market research firm TrendForce has predicted that 80% of TSMC’s production capacity will still be in Taiwan in 2035.

Cost is a major factor in how TSMC divides its investments. Founder Morris Chang has said that it costs 50% more to make semiconductors in the U.S. than in Taiwan, though Canada-based TechInsights has estimated the gap to be less than 10% in light of recent advances in automation.

TSMC plans to build a total of six fabs in the U.S., five in Kaohsiung and four in Hsinchu. It has not provided time frames for completion of these investments, giving the company room to adjust its strategy as needed.

item.title: Thailand weighs cut to tourist visa waiver as cons outweigh pros
item.description:
Extended 60-day window brings limited traffic boost while fueling concerns of abuse

BANGKOK — Thailand is considering reversing its decision to extend visa-free stays for tourists to up to 60 days last year, in response to a lower-than-hoped boost to traffic as well as concerns over individuals who abuse the system.

Minister of Tourism and Sports Sorawong Thienthong revealed the plans in mid-March. Details are expected to be finalized at a later cabinet meeting.

Thailand’s tourism industry accounts for almost 20% of its gross domestic product. To further boost tourist numbers, it expanded visa-free entry for tourists from 57 to 93 countries in July. The maximum stay for passport holders from many countries, including Japan, was also extended from 30 days to 60 days.

But the effect of the changes has been smaller than hoped. While the number of foreign tourists who visited Thailand in 2024 was about 36 million — reaching around 90% of pre-pandemic figures — some believe it will take several more years to hit the 40 million mark due to the economic downturn in China and other factors.

The average length of stay by tourists was also around 20 days, indicating that relatively few are taking advantage of the extended 60-day cap.

Meanwhile, the relaxed restrictions have turned the spotlight on related illegal activities, such as foreigners renting rooms out to tourists without proper authorization. The Thai Travel Agents Association has raised alarm over such cases.

Concerns are also growing about foreigners becoming ensnared in scams in Thailand. Thailand’s security situation has come under scrutiny since January when a Chinese national was kidnapped after entering Thailand and then held captive in a Myanmar scam center.

Thailand has also introduced a digital nomad visa, valid for five years and allowing people to stay for up to 180 days at a time. While its purpose is to secure talented workers and increase consumption in the country, it may further diminish the need for tourist visa waivers.

item.title: Japan estimates feared megaquake could kill 300,000, cause $1.8tn in damage
item.description:
Loss would amount to nearly half of country's GDP

TOKYO (Reuters) — Japan’s economy could lose as much as $1.81 trillion in the event of a long-anticipated megaquake off its Pacific coast, which could trigger devastating tsunamis, the collapse of hundreds of buildings and potentially kill about 300,000 people, a government report said on Monday.

The expected economic damage of 270.3 trillion yen, or nearly half of the country’s total gross domestic product, was up sharply from the previous estimate of 214.2 trillion yen as the new estimate accounted for inflationary pressures and updated terrain and ground data which have expanded anticipated flood areas, the Cabinet Office report showed.

Japan is one of the world’s most earthquake-prone countries, and the government sees about an 80% chance of a magnitude-8 to -9 earthquake along a tremulous seabed zone known as the Nankai Trough.

Under the worst-case scenario, based on a potential magnitude-9 earthquake in the area, Japan is likely to see 1.23 million evacuees, or 1% of its total population. As many as 298,000 people could die from tsunamis and building collapses if the quake occurs late at night in winter, the report showed.

The trough is off Japan’s southwest Pacific coast and runs for approximately 900 kilometers (600 miles), where the Philippine Sea Plate is subducting under the Eurasian Plate. The accumulating tectonic strains could result in a megaquake roughly once in 100 to 150 years.

Last year, Japan issued its first-ever megaquake advisory that there was a “relatively higher chance” of a quake as powerful as magnitude 9 in the trough, after a magnitude-7.1 quake occurred at the edge of the trough.

A magnitude-9 quake in 2011 that triggered a devastating tsunami and the triple reactor meltdowns at a nuclear power plant in northeast Japan killed more than 15,000 people.

item.title: Power semiconductor tech cuts energy loss 30%, Japan group says
item.description:
Joint research holds promise for making electric vehicles more efficient

TOKYO — Researchers in Japan have developed technology to reduce electricity loss by as much as 30% in power semiconductor devices.

The team led by Makoto Takamiya, a professor at the University of Tokyo’s Institute of Industrial Science, created a sensor circuit that detects voltage in a power semiconductor, as well as technology to automatically adjust current to the detected value.

These reduce power loss when the semiconductor switches current voltage and frequency. The new technology is said to be compatible with most power semiconductors on the market.

Power semiconductors are essential components for electric vehicles and other applications, with separate driver semiconductors also required.

The drivers usually operate the power semiconductors via simple mechanical actions to change current strength, with the lack of flexibility making the process prone to wasting energy.

The new technology reduces power loss during the switching process by up to 30%. But power loss can also be due to electrical resistance, so the total loss reduction throughout the semiconductor comes to 6%.

Previously, precise current detection and controls were available for only certain power semiconductors. Because power semiconductors integrate multiple circuits, it is expected that the newly designed devices can be made at small size and at low cost. The research team is working with semiconductor manufacturers to commercialize the new technology.

The technology is the fruit of joint research with Tokyo’s Shibaura Institute of Technology. The findings were presented at the Applied Power Electronics Conference, held in the U.S. from March 16 through March 20.

item.title: China eyes ex-vice finance minister to lead Asia infrastructure bank
item.description:
Zou Jiayi would become 2nd chief of Beijing-led AIIB

BEIJING — China has nominated Zou Jiayi, a former vice finance minister, as a candidate for the next president of the China-led Asian Infrastructure Investment Bank, the Finance Ministry said on Monday.

The AIIB is expected to elect its next president at an annual meeting in Beijing in June. Zou, who hails from Jiangsu province, was in charge of international affairs at the Finance Ministry. She has worked for many years at international financial institutions such as the World Bank and the Asian Development Bank.

The term of office for the AIIB president is five years. If elected, Zou would take office in January 2026. Jin Liqun, who has served as president since the bank’s opening in 2016, will step down.

China holds the most shares in the AIIB at 30%. The bank, which invests in infrastructure across Asia, has more than 100 member countries and regions, but Japan and the U.S. are not included.

item.title: U.S. court suspends Florida ban on colleges hiring students from China
item.description:
Judge determines state's restriction conflicts with federal immigration law

NEW YORK — A federal court has granted a preliminary injunction against part of a Florida law that restricts the employment of students from China and six other countries in the state’s public universities, a move welcomed by Asian American groups amid heightened U.S. scrutiny of Chinese people.

U.S. District Judge Jose Martinez ruled on Friday, in agreement with the magistrate judge, that foreigners already granted student visas will not be affected by the state law, commonly known as SB 846, and that the legislation conflicted with federal immigration law.

SB 846 bars the state government from hiring anyone living in China, North Korea, Iran, Russia, Cuba, Syria and Venezuela. It applies to faculty members at the state’s 12 public universities trying to hire graduate and postdoctoral students for research. Such individuals seeking employment would need to prove to Florida governing bodies that they are not national security threats, the American Civil Liberties Union of Florida reports.

SB 846 was passed unanimously by Florida’s legislature in 2023 in a bid to address foreign interference in academia and as part of an ongoing campaign by Gov. Ron DeSantis against alleged Chinese Communist Party influence in the U.S.

Critics say the law is discriminatory and restricts academic freedom.

Two Chinese students at Florida International University, Yin Zhipeng and Guo Zhen, as well as University of Florida professor Guan Zhengfei filed a lawsuit against the Florida Board of Governors and other state education officials last year arguing that SB 846 violates federal immigration law as well as equal protection and due process rights.

The lawsuit also alleged that the restrictions have affected Guan’s ability to recruit and hire the best postdoctoral candidates.

The judge said Yin and Guo have been personally harmed by the law, but disagreed that it discriminates against them based on their ethnicity.

“The law’s focus is not on race, ancestry, or national origin, but country of domicile,” the judge wrote.

The judge added that federal immigration law bars the state from determining eligibility for employment on the basis of national security concerns and a foreign student’s country.

The injunction allows the two students to be granted the teaching assistantships they were offered and suspends enforcement of the law until a court hearing on whether the law should be overturned.

“This decision confirms our belief that the Florida law is unconstitutional and should not be enforced. Florida’s xenophobia against Chinese has no factual basis and should not be tolerated,” said Clay Zhu of the Chinese American Legal Defense Alliance, which is representing the plaintiffs along with the ACLU of Florida and law firm Perkins Coie.

The Florida Department of Education appealed the decision.

The Florida law is one of many pieces of legislation in states around the U.S. that target Chinese nationals, such as by barring them from buying land. A bill introduced in Congress in March would halt visas for student and research visas for Chinese citizens.

The federal ruling comes as the U.S. tightens immigration and cracks down on foreign students and undocumented immigrants.

Yunseo Chung, a Columbia University student, was sought by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement in March when the Trump administration intensified efforts to deport noncitizens who participated in campus protests that the government deems antisemitic. A federal judge in Manhattan ruled last week that Chung cannot be taken into immigration detention.

item.title: Mizuho exits global climate group, leaving one Japanese lender
item.description:
Major financial group says it achieved aims under Net-Zero Banking Alliance

TOKYO — Mizuho Financial Group has decided to withdraw from an international alliance of banks committed to combating climate change, joining an exodus of Japanese members from the decarbonization framework.

On Monday, Mizuho notified the Net-Zero Banking Alliance that it will leave the group. The bank said it has achieved the objectives that were set at the time it joined NZBA.

Five out of six Japanese financial groups have now exited NZBA, including Sumitomo Mitsui Financial Group and leading brokerage Nomura Holdings. Sumitomo Mitsui Trust Group is the only one remaining.

NZBA is an industry-led framework in which members aim to attain net-zero greenhouse gas emissions by 2050 through their lending, investment and capital market activities. The alliance was established in April 2021, and Mizuho joined in October the same year.

But since the election of U.S. President Donald Trump, NZBA’s cross-industry activities have received mounting criticism.

Six global banks including JPMorgan Chase and Goldman Sachs have announced their departures from the alliance since December. The Royal Bank of Canada also has stated its withdrawal.

Mizuho has adopted a transition plan toward decarbonization, as well as metrics that track greenhouse gas reduction throughout the lender’s financing and investment chain, including business partners. The bank plans to continue with its decarbonization efforts even after withdrawing from NZBA.

item.title: Toyota unit Hino faces lawsuit in New Zealand over engine data
item.description:
Japanese truck maker's woes could impact Mitsubishi Fuso Truck and Bus merger talks

TOKYO — Hino Motors said Monday it is facing litigation from three New Zealand companies that are seeking damages over the Japanese truck maker’s falsification of engine data.

The companies, which filed a lawsuit in the High Court of New Zealand, are representing users of Hino trucks purchased or exchanged in New Zealand between 2010 and 2025. They claim that they suffered damages from Hino’s violation of engine fuel efficiency standards.

The amount claimed in the lawsuit has not been disclosed.

Hino, a Toyota Motor subsidiary, and its local sales company are the targets of the lawsuit. The company “cannot rule out that other similar types of proceedings may be filed against Hino in the future,” Hino said in a statement.

Hino was found in 2022 to have falsified data in emissions and fuel efficiency tests. New Zealand is the fourth country where the company has faced litigation, following the U.S., Australia and Canada.

The scandal was thought to have come to an end after the company reached a settlement with U.S. authorities in January.

In 2023, Hino reached a basic agreement to merge with Mitsubishi Fuso Truck and Bus, a subsidiary of Germany’s Daimler Truck. But the deal has since been postponed indefinitely amid the fallout from the scandal.

Hino did not comment on the impact of the New Zealand litigation on the merger talks.

item.title: Thai Airways seeks to regain its wings as it exits bankruptcy rehab
item.description:
Flag carrier will shed baggage of state enterprise past, executives say

BANGKOK — Gone are the days when Thai Airways flight crews waltzed through Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport in purple suits before changing into traditional silk dresses upon boarding. Now, they don only one outfit, a sustainability initiative that also doubled as a cost-cutting measure.

Getting rid of the outfit change was the most visible reform at Thai Airways during its five-year rehabilitation from bankruptcy. Behind the scenes, the workforce is leaner by nearly half, its fleet is 23% smaller, and decisions are made more efficiently by professional managers, its top executives told Nikkei Asia.

“Before COVID, I would say that over 50% of the time of the board was spent discussing whether a decision would be in line with this regulation or that regulation,” said Piyasvasti Amranand, chairman of Thai’s rehabilitation administration. “Now I would say that 90% is business. Decisions are made very quickly.”

Piyasvasti and Chai Eamsiri, Thai’s chief executive officer, spoke exclusively with Nikkei Asia ahead of the company’s planned exit from rehabilitation in May. If the exit is approved by the Central Bankruptcy Court, next quarter would end a long fall from grace for Thailand’s flag carrier that culminated in 2020 when the COVID-19 pandemic decimated tourism and air travel.

Thai’s return to financial health would also mark its emergence from state ownership, vindicating executives whose past business plans were overruled by politically appointed boards. The airline’s fortunes and quick succession of managers tracked the political turmoil that plagued Thailand in the early 2000s.

Already unprofitable in the three years leading up to the pandemic, Thai filed for bankruptcy protection in May 2020 and entered rehabilitation. Under Thai law, when a court approves a company to enter rehabilitation, it is allowed to restructure its assets and liabilities while continuing to operate and have the court mediate between it and its creditors.

Its Bangkok-listed stock has been suspended since May 2021.

“Interference from outside was the beginning of the downturn of the company,” Piyasvasti said. After Thai’s rehabilitation, “It will not become a state enterprise. That is something the government has made clear.”

Although the Ministry of Finance is still the largest shareholder at 38.9%, the government’s total stake has fallen to 42% under the rehabilitation plan, below the 50% threshold that defines state-owned enterprises. Creditors like Bangkok Bank, Krungthai Bank and TMBThanachart Bank each hold less than 10%.

Piyasvasti returned to Thai as rehabilitation administrator in 2020, after his tenure as a reformist CEO was cut short by a boardroom coup in 2012. The Pheu Thai party was in power again, and Piyasvasti had served as energy minister under military leaders who ousted Prime Minister Thaksin Shinawatra, Pheu Thai’s founder, in 2006.

Thai Airways cabin attendants at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport. The crew now no longer change outfits when they board the aircraft, part of the airline’s cost-cutting measures. (Photo by Yuki Kohara)

Professional managers like Chai, a 40-year veteran of the company, were also frustrated as their recommendations were regularly overruled by board directors citing government regulations.

For example, government rules prevented the company from selling old planes at a loss on their book value, even if certain models proved uneconomical. Doing so would have triggered an investigation by Thailand’s auditor general or the anti-corruption commission, said Piyasvasti.

Under rehabilitation, the airline was able to trim its fleet from 103 to 79, with a smaller range of models. Employees, previously protected by government staffing rules, were offered voluntary layoff packages. Thai once had the highest ratio of employees to aircraft among Asian airlines, but has shed nearly half of its workforce down to about 17,000.

The improved cost structure, executives say, has given Thai room to adjust salaries to attract high-quality talent.

“In the past, personnel costs represented about 23%,” Chai said. “Now we have reduced it to under 12%. That’s not because we’re cutting benefits or salaries, but because we’re working smarter. We’re using less people and more digital processes.”

The new salary structure has not been finalized, but Chai said personnel costs would remain less than 12% even with the planned salary increases, a lower rate than many airlines.

Still, the air travel market is just as competitive as it was when Thai Airways entered bankruptcy protection, with the rapid expansion of regional low-cost airlines. In 2023, Thai AirAsia led the domestic market with 36.9% of scheduled flights, while Thai Airways has declined to 0.9% from 7.6% in 2019.

Efforts to introduce a lower-cost subsidiary, Thai Smile, in 2011 faltered as its costs were higher than the likes of rivals AirAsia and Jetstar. Thai Smile and its parent also cannibalized each other’s business, due to different booking systems and separate management. Thai Smile ceased operations and was fully merged into Thai Airways at the start of last year, adding short-haul aircraft to the prestige airline’s fleet.

The new Thai Airways would not seek to compete with low-cost carriers, the executives said. “We are not lowering our price to compete with them, because they are in a different market segment and we are full-service,” Chai said. “We know our strength is bringing passengers from outside Thailand into Bangkok, and then connecting them to various domestic and regional destinations.”

But the pent-up demand for travel after the pandemic — which has kept airfares high and airline margins wide — will run out eventually. The Thai airline industry will recover to pre-COVID levels this year, according to Krungsri Research.

Chai said supply chain issues in aviation will persist. Production delays at the two biggest aircraft makers, Boeing and Airbus, as well as their engine supplies, have created a shortage of planes. This will prevent airlines like Thai from increasing routes and fully meeting travel demand in the near future. “We’re talking about three, four years before the normal supply chain can come back,” he said.

Thai Airways aircraft at Bangkok’s Suvarnabhumi Airport. The airline has reduced its number of airplanes by 23% in recent years as it undertakes its rehabilitation. (Photo by Yuki Kohara)

“Our problem at the moment is really that we don’t have enough aircraft,” Piyasvasti added. “The aircraft we have leased or ordered new are being delayed. We are not really opening new destinations yet, so there is still a lot of room, I think, for more revenue.”

To exit rehabilitation, Thai Airways had to deliver at least 20 billion baht in annual earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization. The company reported more than 40 billion baht in EBITDA for the past two consecutive fiscal years.

Its debt has eased from 338 billion baht at the end of 2020, to 247 billion baht in 2024. Long-term liabilities, the largest portion, decreased by 21.7% from the previous year, after the company issued new shares and allocated them to creditors in a debt-to-equity swap at the end of 2024. Deferred revenue on advance ticket sales and long-term provisions for aircraft maintenance make up most of the remaining debt.

The next step is electing a new board on April 18. In November, the Thai Airways workers’ union called on creditors to vote against two nominees from the Finance and Transport Ministries to fill the government’s seat quota, raising concerns of renewed political interference.

“Involvement from the government is more concerning to investors than the remaining debt,” said Dithanop Vattanawakin, an analyst at Krungsri Securities. “If the government quota is larger than the private sector directors, there’s a risk that past mistakes could recur.”

Chai said the slate of nominees would have backgrounds in digital technology, legal affairs, human resources and foreign exchange and fuel hedging. “Those are the areas where the company needs people with expertise.”

The airline plans to resume trading on the Stock Exchange of Thailand in June, after the board election in April and a court-approved exit from rehabilitation. Most Thai securities houses have not covered Thai Airways since it was suspended from the bourse in 2021, but analysts are skeptical that banks and retirement funds can forgive and forget the negative returns on Thai bonds.

“I’d be very surprised if there’s strong demand,” said Dean Ginnane, director of technology at Baker Tilly Thailand. “This is a stock that has consistently let people down. If it starts performing and becoming profitable, people might have short memories and forget about the past.”

Chai acknowledged the need to rebuild trust not only with investors but also with passengers and employees. That would hinge on turning its strengths — Thailand’s status as a tourism hot spot and the airline’s strong recognizable brand — into results.

New and leased planes have been ordered to bring the fleet back up to 100, while existing planes will be refurbished to increase comfort and reintroduce inflight entertainment.

And while it will not return to state ownership, Chai said the airline would remain an ambassador for the country: “When we fly to other countries, we are the first company to welcome foreigners into Thailand, and we are the last to send them home. No one else can do this.”

item.title: Renault, Nissan loosen ties further to aid Japan automaker’s turnaround
item.description:
Cross-shareholdings to shrink; Nissan no longer required to invest in EV unit Ampere

PARIS (Reuters) — Automakers Renault and Nissan Motor said on Monday they had agreed to further amend their two-decade-old partnership to allow for a reduction in their cross-shareholdings in a move aimed at helping Nissan’s recovery.

The change in terms, lowering the required shareholding to 10% from 15% previously, comes a day before Ivan Espinosa takes over as CEO of the struggling Japanese carmaker, under pressure to significantly boost its competitiveness.

Nissan will also be released from its commitment to invest in Renault’s electric vehicle unit Ampere, for which it had pledged 600 million euros ($649 million).

“As a longtime partner of Nissan within the alliance and as its main shareholder, Renault Group has a strong interest in seeing Nissan turn around its performance as quickly as possible,” said Renault CEO Luca de Meo in a statement.

Renault also announced its intention to buy out Nissan’s majority stake in their joint Indian business, Renault Nissan Automotive India Private Ltd. (RNAIPL), with the expected completion of the deal by the end of the first half of this year.

As a result, Nissan will cease making cars in the world’s third-largest auto market and will focus on sales and service.

Renault will continue to make cars for Nissan at the venture’s factory in India’s southern state of Tamil Nadu. The plant can produce over 400,000 cars a year but is only running at about a third of that capacity, industry data shows.

“Nissan is committed to preserving the value and benefits of our strategic partnership within the Alliance while implementing turnaround measures to enhance efficiencies,” said incoming CEO Espinosa in the statement.

Espinosa, previously Nissan’s chief planning officer, was appointed in early March to succeed Makoto Uchida, after deteriorating results at Japan’s third-largest automaker and unsuccessful negotiations for a merger with Honda Motor.

Nissan, in which Renault is the largest shareholder with 17.05% of the capital held directly, has been plagued for years by declining sales.

It has struggled to recover from the downfall of former boss Carlos Ghosn, architect of the Renault-Nissan alliance, who was accused by the Tokyo prosecutor’s office of financial misconduct, which he denies.

Renault confirmed its forecast of free cash flow of at least 2 billion euros in 2025, despite an impact of approximately 200 million euros from acquiring Nissan’s stake in the Indian business.

“The decision today gives Nissan additional flexibility, which would be the possibility for Nissan to sell assets and increase their cash position,” Renault CFO Duncan Minto told journalists. He said having such ability would help Nissan restructure.

The amendment to the alliance agreement, which in 2023 established a rebalancing of cross-shareholdings, and the termination of Nissan’s investment agreement in Ampere, are subject to certain preconditions being fulfilled, expected by the end of May, the companies said.

item.title: Hong Kong retail sales fall 12 straight months as Shenzhen rivalry stings
item.description:
February figure sinks 13% as locals cross border and mainland visitors spend less

HONG KONG — Retail sales in Hong Kong fell for the 12th straight month in February, underscoring the plight of merchants and hotels as local residents flock across the border to Shenzhen while mainland travelers rein in spending in the city.

The city’s census and statistics department tallied 29.4 billion Hong Kong dollars ($3.77 billion) of retail sales in February, down 13% on the year and much steeper than January’s 3.1% drop. It was the first figure in double digits since last August.

A spokesperson for the city’s government partly attributed the plunge to the earlier Lunar New Year in late January, versus mid-February 2024. Even so, the decline of Hong Kong’s retail sales across the first two months of 2025 came to 9.9%.

The government is pinning hopes for a turnaround on Beijing’s economic stimulus policies as well as local tourism promotion campaigns. But the spokesperson conceded that Hong Kong’s retail sector “would continue to face challenges from the change in consumption patterns of visitors and residents.”

Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels, the operator of the luxury Peninsula Hotels chain, said the same day that it sees “a gradual improvement in the overall tourism sentiment in Hong Kong.” But the hotel chain was wary of conditions in the food and beverage industry, where it “continued to be negatively impacted by a trend of Hong Kong residents traveling to the neighboring city of Shenzhen to experience alternative dining options and hotel stays.”

The company said that its flagship Peninsula Hong Kong hotel’s revenue rose by 3% on the year in 2024 to reach HK$1.06 billion, with room occupancy up by 6 percentage points. Nevertheless, the average room rate fell by 5% and was still 20% lower than in 2018, before anti-government demonstrations swept the city in 2019 and the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020.

Hong Kong’s storied Peninsula hotel: The operator’s CEO acknowledged that “geopolitical tensions remain a general concern.”   © Getty Images

Benjamin Vuchot — who became CEO of the group on March 3 after his predecessor Clement Kwok stepped down last October, after 22 years on the job — said in a statement that the flow of long-haul leisure travelers from the U.S. and Europe that the hotel traditionally relied upon “is improving.” Yet, he also noted that “geopolitical tensions remain a general concern.”

Assessing the trajectory is slightly more difficult now because, despite the Peninsula Hong Kong’s 159 years of history, the operator abolished the overall “Hong Kong” segment in the latest annual earnings — which also included other businesses — and from its quarterly disclosure on hotel operations, merging it with Shanghai and Beijing to create a new “Greater China” category.

A company spokesperson told Nikkei Asia that, after the chain’s first full year of operating three hotels in Europe, “it was decided to disclose the results per region on a quarterly basis and include Hong Kong in Greater China.” The spokesperson said basic operational data would still be reported by hotels including the Peninsula Hong Kong on an annual and semi-annual basis.

Overall, the hotel chain reported a net loss of HK$943 million for 2024, reversing from a net profit of HK$146 million a year earlier. This was mainly due to a full write-off of its Yangon hotel project, stalled since June 2021, after the Myanmar military ousted the democratically elected government led by Aung San Suu Kyi.

Regarding the devastating earthquake that hit Myanmar, the spokesperson told Nikkei Asia that all local staff were safe and that there was no structural damage to the property, adding that the disaster “will not affect the future of the project.”

Among Hong Kong businesses more broadly, department stores suffered a particularly heavy blow, with sales falling 21.3% in February.

Wing On Company International reported on March 25 that its department store segment’s sales dropped by 15.1% to HK$542.59 million, while the segment’s loss swelled to HK$60.04 million from HK$2.80 million a year ago.

Chairman Karl Kwok Chi-leung said in the disclosure that this was mainly due to “the changing shopping habits of local residents and the increase in outbound travel and cross-border consumption and spending.”

The 117-year old department store operator had launched “aggressive promotional campaigns with deep discounts throughout 2024 to stimulate sales and reduce inventory,” but these did not translate into more revenue as stores were “affected by the low customer traffic and weak consumer spending.”

“The Hong Kong retail sector has taken longer than anticipated to recover due to persistent economic challenges and shifting consumer preferences,” Kwok said. The company expects to “encounter challenges in 2025, primarily due to the ongoing retail downturn, the sluggish property market performance and geopolitical tensions.”

Chung Wai-ping, chairman and CEO of restaurant and bakery chain operator Tao Heung Holdings, said in the company’s disclosure on March 26 that “the past 12 months have remained a highly challenging period.” The company reported a 17.8% drop in annual revenue to HK$2.42 billion, while sinking to a net loss of HK$52.8 million, reversing from a net profit of HK$73.7 million in 2023.

Tao Heung’s Hong Kong operation, which contributes about two-thirds of its total revenue, “continued to face numerous obstacles in 2024,” according to Chung. He noted that while residents were heading to Shenzhen on weekends, “on weeknights most prefer staying in.”

To try to drum up sales, the company introduced promotions like a dollar dish series, buy-one-get-one-free offers and HK$9.9 late-night hotpot offering. “While they have been well-received by customers and helped maintain our top line, profitability has inevitably been affected,” Chung said.

As of March 26, the group had slimmed down to 85 outlets, slashing 11 from the year before.

item.title: Renault to buy Nissan’s stake in Indian manufacturing unit
item.description:
Renault Nissan Automotive India will be fully owned by Renault Group

(Reuters) — Renault Group said on Monday it would acquire the remaining 51% shareholding in Renault Nissan Automotive India, currently held by Nissan Motor, taking complete ownership of the manufacturing plant.

Located in the southern Indian city of Chennai, RNAIPL began operations in 2010, with Paris-based Renault and Japan-based Nissan holding a 30% and 70% stake, respectively.

Nissan’s stake was reduced to 51% as part of a deal in 2023 to jointly invest $600 million to make six new models in India.

item.title: Panel concludes ex-TV host Nakai did sexually assault Fuji TV staff
item.description:
Committee also points to 'low understanding of human-rights' in handling of case

TOKYO (Kyodo) — A third-party panel probing a scandal involving famous former TV host Masahiro Nakai and its handling by Fuji Television Network has concluded he sexually assaulted a female employee amid a culture of harassment at the company, a report showed Monday.

Fuji TV has been mired in scandal over its response to the case, after a weekly magazine in December reported Nakai engaged in nonconsensual sexual activity and paid a 90 million yen ($600,000) out-of-court settlement to the woman who met him for a dinner in June 2023.

Many companies pulled their advertisements from the network after it faced criticism for its response. Nakai continued to appear in shows for around a year and a half even after senior executives including then President Koichi Minato were aware of the case.

The independent committee was established in mid-January and made up of three lawyers.

It said a “serious infringement of human rights occurred,” and called the incident involving the woman, who worked as an on-screen talent for the company, as sexual violence “occurring as an extension of her job.”

The panel was not in a position to say whether Nakai’s actions constituted a criminal case, its head Akira Takeuchi said in a press conference.

According to their findings, the woman said she agreed to meet Nakai for dinner on the assumption others would be present. When it later became clear they would be meeting alone at his home, she said she felt unable to cancel over concerns it could have a negative impact on her career.

Nakai, who rose to prominence as a member of the now-defunct pop group SMAP, was a famous television host before retiring from showbusiness over the scandal in January.

“Owing to Nakai’s position as major talent for Fuji TV,” there was an “overwhelming difference in authority (between him and the woman),” the panel said.

The panel said it found no evidence that an employee at the firm had arranged the meeting between the two, as first reported and then later retracted by a weekly magazine.

But probe lead Akira Takeuchi told reporters there was a “persistent culture of sexual harassment at Fuji TV,” and that victims did not trust their claims to be reported to its compliance department.

Regarding the TV station’s handling of the case, the report said it “shows a low understanding of sexual violence and human-rights awareness,” and that ex-president Minato treated the case as “a man-woman problem.”

Minato told reporters in January that senior management did not share details of the incident with its compliance department to prioritize the woman’s physical and mental recovery and protect her privacy. He resigned as president days later.

As part of changes to Fuji TV’s executive structure, the firm said Thursday its longtime executive managing adviser Hisashi Hieda, who had a strong influence on its management, has stepped down.

item.title: Japan parliament passes FY 2025 budget after rare revision
item.description:
Ishiba's minority government enlists opposition to navigate difficult path

TOKYO (Kyodo) — Japan’s parliament on Monday enacted a state budget for the next fiscal year after a rare upper house revision reflecting Prime Minister Shigeru Ishiba’s decision to reverse course on a planned hike in medical costs, handing a hard-won victory to the minority government with less than a day remaining in the current fiscal year.

It is the first time under the country’s current Constitution that a budget has been enacted after a revision was approved by the House of Councillors and then the House of Representatives. The total size of the fiscal 2025 budget came to a record 115.20 trillion yen ($770 billion).

Although the ruling Liberal Democratic Party-Komeito party coalition lost its majority in the powerful lower house in last year’s election, the opposition Japan Innovation Party backed the revision, ensuring the budget’s passage.

Lower house decisions on key matters such as budgets take precedence over those of the upper house. When a draft budget plan submitted by the government clears the lower house, it usually means the enactment of that budget is guaranteed.
