The budget enactment should come as a relief to Ishiba as public support rates for his Cabinet hit new lows due to revelations that he handed out gift vouchers worth 100,000 yen each to rookie LDP lower house members in early March.

This brought questions from the public about whether such gift-giving has been a long-held practice among LDP prime ministers, putting further pressure on the ruling party, which is already attempting to paper over a damaging slush fund scandal before the upcoming upper house election this summer.

Faced with navigating minority rule, Ishiba has underlined the importance of listening to demands from opposition parties and incorporating them into policy whenever possible, given the ruling coalition needs their support to pass bills and budgets in the lower house.

Soon after the lower house approved the fiscal budget plan with opposition amendments in early March, Ishiba abruptly shelved a plan to raise medical costs following resistance from opposition lawmakers and patients. The about-face necessitated another change to the budget.

In negotiations to get the budget through the lower house the first time, the ruling camp agreed to accept a request from the Japan Innovation Party to expand subsidies to make high school education tuition free. It also agreed to a Democratic Party for the People demand that the income threshold for tax payments be raised.

The decision to scrap the increase in medical costs was demanded by the main opposition Constitutional Democratic Party of Japan.

About a third of the fiscal 2025 budget will go to social security spending. Japan also plans to spend a record 8.7 trillion yen on defense in the face of growing security threats from its neighbors China and North Korea.

The budget also includes steps to mitigate the pain of rising prices, measures that the government believes are necessary despite Japan seeing its strongest wage growth in decades.

When Ishiba’s remarks underscoring the need for “powerful” inflation-relief steps were revealed last week by the head of Komeito, some opposition lawmakers expressed concern he was hinting at the need for further spending to address cost of living pressures. Ishiba, however, assured them that he was not implying further budgetary measures will be needed.

Even after the budget is passed, Ishiba will continue to face challenges as opposition parties are expected to pressure him and the LDP over the acceptance of corporate donations. The party has yet to shake the issue that came to light when the LDP’s underreporting of political funds was revealed.

The parties are divided over whether to strengthen regulations or to ban such donations outright.

item.title: Shares of Thai firm building tower that collapsed in quake fall 27%
item.description:
Investigation underway into design, quality of China-backed government building

BANGKOK — Shares of Bangkok-listed contractor Italian-Thai Development (ITD) fell 27% on Monday, after a government office tower that it was constructing in the capital with a Chinese partner collapsed following an earthquake on Friday.

Eleven people died in the collapse, while 76 are unaccounted for, presumed trapped in the rubble. The casualty figures for the whole city are 18 dead, 33 injured and 78 missing.

The Thai government has launched a probe into the design and quality of materials used in the 30-story State Audit Office tower. Investigators are analyzing the steel bars used. Substandard steel bars would not be able to withstand an earthquake, according to the Ministry of Industry, especially not the force of the 7.7-magnitude temblor that shook Myanmar and Thailand on Friday.

Italian-Thai, a longtime government contractor, was working on the project with a subsidiary of China Railway No. 10 Engineering Group. Debt and liquidity problems have affected ITD since the COVID-19 pandemic, with the company postponing debenture payments last year as the government budget was delayed by a prolonged postelection impasse.

ITD depends on government contracts for a larger portion of its revenue than Sino-Thai Engineering & Construction and CH Karnchang, the two other big Bangkok-listed developers, and had in the last fiscal year weaker earnings and less diversified investments. ITD opened down 27% and stayed around there all day. CHK fell 3.5% but Sino-Thai ended the day up 2.8% after erasing early morning losses. The Thai stock index closed 1.5% lower.

The Bangkok Metropolitan Administration assured city residents on Sunday evening that it had responded to most crowd-sourced building safety reports, and that public transportation infrastructure was structurally sound. City officials have deployed more than 100 volunteer engineers to conduct emergency inspections since Friday. The capital’s elevated and underground rapid transit systems returned to service on Saturday morning, after shutting down immediately after the quake.

“As of last night, there are approximately 13,000 complaints about building safety, of which around 10,000 have already been examined, and 2,000 are pending and will be processed today. Out of [the] 10,000, most are labeled green. Only two buildings are labeled red,” Thanes Weerasiri, president of the Council of Engineers of Thailand, said Monday. Red buildings are severely damaged, while green buildings are considered safe to reenter.

A man walks past the headquarters of the Italian-Thai Development Public Company in Bangkok. The firm, with a Chinese partner, was building the 30-story State Audit Office tower that collapsed in the earthquake on March 28. (Photo by Yuki Kohara)

Thanes added, “In most of the cases we’ve inspected, the damage is only cracks in the wall and the surfaces, not at the structural level, which is normal. This means we have passed a major test for our ministerial regulation standard.”

People in Bangkok remained jittery on Monday. Residents and office workers in Asok and Phrom Phong, downtown neighborhoods, were advised to evacuate at midday as the Meteorological Department warned of aftershocks.

Earlier, a nine-story building at a large government complex in the north of the city housing the Constitutional Court and Central Bankruptcy Court was evacuated after tremors, cracked walls and falling debris were reported.

Prime Minister Paetongtarn Shinawatra took to X at noon to dispel public panic. “The Meteorological Department reported that there was no earthquake in Thailand and the aftershock from Myanmar did not affect Thailand at all,” she wrote, reiterating the order for building owners to urgently inspect buildings for cracks.

While Bangkok itself is not prone to earthquakes, and the epicenter was more than 1,000 kilometers away, the Thai capital is sensitive to tremors because of its soft clay underlayer. Still, glass skyscrapers crowd the city, including the 77-story Mahanakhon Tower, which visibly swayed in the earthquake on Friday. Aside from the State Audit Office tower, no other building in Bangkok collapsed as a result of the quake.

Interior Minister Anutin Charnvirakul said he was instructing all owners to recertify their buildings outside of the annual inspection.

But the capital’s condominium market may suffer from buyer hesitation at a time when critical policies are being rolled out to support public housing and the real estate sector. The Bank of Thailand’s loan-to-value (LTV) easing policy, scheduled to begin on May 1 and run for 14 months, had been expected to stimulate real estate investment and improve market sentiment.

The number of new condo units rose 68% in the first quarter of 2025 from the same period a year earlier, a sign of recovery in the market. But postquake buyer hesitation could increase the volume of unsold inventory, estimated by real estate consultancy Colliers to be worth 458 billion baht ($13.5 billion).
item.author: FRANCESCA REGALADO

item.title: China’s big bank shares mixed after $72bn capital injection unveiled
item.description:
Finance ministry says funding will help institutions be 'main force' for economy

HONG KONG — Shares of China’s top state banks were mixed on Monday after four of them announced plans the day before to raise a combined 520 billion yuan ($71.7 billion) by issuing new shares amid a broad market sell-off.

The four banks — China Construction Bank, Bank of China, Bank of Communications and Postal Savings Bank of China — all opened higher on mainland exchanges. The stocks temporarily wobbled, with BoCom slipping into negative territory, before they all closed up. The CSI 300 Index, a gauge of mainland-listed stocks, fell 0.7%.

The banks’ Hong Kong-listed shares were more volatile, with CCB rising nearly 3% but PSBC falling more than 3%. The Industrial and Commercial Bank of China and Agricultural Bank of China, which are part of the “big six” state banks but did not announce capital injection plans, fell before rebounding. The benchmark Hang Seng Index fell 1.3% as concerns over an escalating trade war rippled across global markets.

After the market closed, representatives for the four banks held an online text exchange with investors. They fielded questions on subjects ranging from the necessity of the share issuance and future dividend policy to protection of minority shareholders and the difference in the premiums given to the new shares over Friday’s closing share prices.

A representative for CCB wrote that it was included in the “first batch” of capital injections, while BoCom said it expects the government to eventually support all six major state banks, including ICBC and ABC.

China’s Ministry of Finance will issue 500 billion yuan in special treasury bonds and use the proceeds to buy up the banks’ new shares. Chinese Premier Li Qiang announced plans to issue the bonds at the National People’s Congress earlier this month as part of a package of stimulus policies to boost the economy.

The remaining 20 billion yuan will come from state-owned enterprises including China Mobile, China State Shipbuilding Corporation and China Tobacco.

Shujin Chen, an analyst at Jefferies, wrote in a report on Sunday that banks with relatively weaker capital are getting more funding, with BoCom and PSBC facing the most dilutions to their dividends per share.

The four institutions will use the proceeds to replenish their core tier-1 capital, which analysts say should help them to increase lending amid record-low interest rates. In 2024 earnings results announced last week, the net interest margin (NIM) — a key gauge of profitability — fell at all four banks.

Executives at some of the banks said they expect their NIMs to come under further pressure this year, because the central bank has said it will make “timely” cuts to interest rates. Boosting consumption is a top priority for the Chinese government as it races to restore confidence weakened by a prolonged property market downturn and grim job prospects.

Analysts at Citi also flagged the government’s capital injection into large lenders as preparation for a “potential small bank bailout” if defaults become widespread.

The share issuance will result in the finance ministry becoming a major holder in the four banks, further tightening the government’s grip on the banking sector. The ministry on Monday said the state-owned banks “are operating in a stable and sound manner.”

Replenishing their core tier-1 capital “will help further strengthen their capacity for sound operations, promote high-quality development, create greater value for investors and deliver long-term and stable returns,” it said. “It will also help the banks better fulfill their role as the main force in serving the real economy.”

The online text exchange signaled some skepticism over the banks’ ability to improve profitability as they come under pressure from policymakers to stimulate the economy. “Do you really feel justified in squandering the capital invested by the vast number of shareholders and the state’s fiscal funds, only to deliver such a low return on equity?” one participant asked.

The question went unanswered.

Additional reporting by Kenji Kawase.

item.title: Tokyo exchange to mandate English disclosure to lure overseas investors
item.description:
Taiwan, South Korea also aim to become more foreign-investor friendly

TOKYO — The Tokyo Stock Exchange (TSE) will require companies listed on its top-tier Prime section of the market to disclose key financial information both in Japanese and English, starting Tuesday, in a move aimed at creating a level playing-field between domestic and overseas investors.

Some 1,600 or so Prime-listed companies are now required to disclose financial results in both Japanese and English at the same time. The rule also applies to information that may have a material effect on investment decisions, such as revisions to earnings forecasts, mergers and acquisitions and changes to representative directors.

“The Prime market is a global market. We have decided to mandate English disclosure from the perspective of attracting more overseas investors,” Sayuri Nakamura at the TSE’s listing department told Nikkei Asia.

Disclosure in English is part of a broader trend among non-English speaking countries in Asia. The Taiwan Stock Exchange, for instance, mandated that all listed companies disclose key information, which is equivalent to Japan’s timely disclosure information, in English by 2024. In South Korea, large KOSPI-listed companies are now required to release material information in English within three days of Korean-language disclosures.

Foreign investors often feel they are at a disadvantage when key documents are released only in local languages.

According to a survey released by the TSE in August 2023, 72% of overseas investors responded that they were “somewhat dissatisfied” or “dissatisfied” on Japanese companies’ English disclosures. “Dissatisfaction mostly comes from the gap in the amount of information in Japanese and English, and also from the time lag of disclosure,” said Nakamura.

The move is part of broader efforts by the TSE to bring the governance standards at Japan Inc. to international levels.

The TSE has introduced a series of measures to raise awareness among Japan’s listed companies about their low stock market valuations, urging companies whose share prices are less than their book value to work harder to raise the valuations.

The efforts have been paying off, as the TSE now hears more overseas investors expressing high expectations for Japanese stocks. “We are also hearing securities firms saying that the tide is turning,” said Natsumi Yamawaki, manager at the listing department at the TSE.

“The challenge is how to maintain positive attention to Japanese companies,” said Yamawaki. “We encourage companies to engage with investors and create a cycle that will increase corporate value,” she said. Her hope is to increase the number of “investors who are committed to companies with a medium- to long-term perspective.”

Naomi Fink, chief global strategist at Nikko Asset Management, said TSE’s request for English disclosure is “very consistent” with what has been already done. The TSE is “putting a large amount of emphasis on disclosure as a whole, and I see English disclosure as part of that.”

“We already have quite a lot of overseas investment in Japanese stocks, and of all overseas investors, there’s quite a few activist investors and those that are putting a lot of emphasis on corporate governance,” Fink pointed out.

“If there isn’t transparent data, then you’re less likely to invest overall. To increase transparency for all investors, especially overseas investors, I think English exposure is a big advantage.

As of the end of December 2024, 99% of listed companies on the Prime market already embraced English disclosure one way or the other, according to a survey by the TSE. However, only 59.2% of companies disclosed their timely disclosure materials in English, compared with 93.8% for financial results and 76.4% for IR presentation materials.

According to the TSE, some companies outsource their translation work, but insist that they need to check the translation for accuracy. Some companies say it is difficult to disclose materials in both languages simultaneously, because the materials are subject to review until the last minute.

Analysts say the question is whether the most relevant information is provided in both languages.

“It is important for companies to consider the introduction of English disclosure as an opportunity to find out which kind of information investors want,” Atsushi Kamio, senior researcher at the Daiwa Institute of Research told Nikkei Asia. He thinks what matters is the disclosure of qualitative information which helps investors judge whether a company can make profits continuously.
item.author: TAMAYO MUTO

item.title: Toyota hopes better biofuels give combustion engine cars new life
item.description:
Ethanol plant tests new production methods using Toyota-made yeast

TOKYO — Japanese carmakers, led by Toyota Motor, are making bioethanol at a research center in northern Japan to encourage use of the plant-based fuel and to reduce the carbon footprint of combustion engine cars. Conventional cars face an uncertain future as electric vehicles gain traction.

In February, the ethanol plant, operated by the Research Association of Biomass Innovation for Next Generation Automobile Fuels, opened in Fukushima prefecture. The research association, created in 2022, counts Toyota, Suzuki Motor, Subaru, Daihatsu Motor, Mazda Motor, Toyota-affiliated trading house Toyota Tsusho and oil company Eneos as members.

Koichi Nakata, chairman of the association and head of Toyota’s carbon-neutral development division, argues the decarbonization effect of carbon-neutral fuels like ethanol compares favorably with EVs. Toyota has been researching biofuels for more than a decade.

“EVs only help cut the CO2 emissions of new cars, but we can lower the emissions of engine [powered] cars currently operating on roads to a certain extent by using carbon-neutral fuel,” Nakata, who has long worked on engines at Toyota, told Nikkei Asia. Bioethanol is already widely used in blends with gasoline and can immediately reduce carbon emissions, said Nakata. The facility’s primary goal is to come up with a sustainable way to make it.

Ethanol is typically derived from food crops like sugarcane and corn, which puts pressure on the food supply. Researchers around the world have been trying to replace such feedstocks with nonedible plants, waste or residues but have struggled with high costs.

A research association led by Toyota Motor has started making bioethanol at a plant in Fukushima prefecture. (The Research Association of Biomass Innovation for Next Generation Automobile Fuels)

One approach that Nakata’s research association will take to tackle this problem is improving the fermentation process that produces alcohol from feedstocks. Instead of using naturally occurring yeast, it will use a special type of yeast developed by Toyota that makes fermentation more efficient. It will also test ways to grow nonedible plants using land in a part of Fukushima that was affected by the Fukushima Daiichi nuclear plant disaster in 2011.

The ethanol plant, which cost 5 billion yen ($33 million) to build, is paid for in part by government subsidies. It can make up to 60 kiloliters of bioethanol a year, enough to keep about 200 Toyota Prius cars on the road. It will initially use sorghum as a feedstock. Operators hope to switch to nonedible feedstock in the future.

According to Nakata, interest is growing in new methods of producing biofuels in countries like Brazil, the world’s second-largest bioethanol producer after the U.S., and India, which is promoting the use of biofuels to lessen its dependence on imported oil.

“I’d be grateful if we could deploy our research results overseas, too, where there is large-scale capacity to make bioethanol using sugarcane or corn,” he said. “Existing large-scale production facilities produce a lot of waste, which we could utilize if we build our plant nearby.”

The focus on bioethanol by carmakers is part of a broader effort to improve the image of combustion engine cars, most of which run on fossil fuel. Automakers like Toyota hope to preserve their competitive edge in engine technology.

“Only internal combustion engines have the potential to become carbon negative,” said Ichiro Hirose, Mazda’s senior managing executive officer. Engines operate by sucking in the air around them, which means they could be developed to capture CO2 in the air, allowing them to act like “an air purifier that moves,” he told Nikkei Asia on the sidelines of a news conference in mid-March.

“We want to show that we will actively continue to work on internal combustion engines and expand their possibilities,” said Hirose. “There is huge potential to save them” in the face of changing technology.
item.author: SAYUMI TAKE

item.title: Pakistan must rethink mass deportations of Afghans
item.description:
Expelling refugees risks deepening a humanitarian crisis and fueling conflict

Farhan Bokhari is an Islamabad-based foreign correspondent who writes on Pakistan and the surrounding region.

As Pakistan moves to deport thousands of undocumented Afghan nationals by the Monday deadline, its actions will be shaped by its strategic interests and the complex realities within Afghanistan.

Pakistan has cited compelling security challenges as a fundamental driver for the decision, notably, militant separatists’ audacious hijacking of a train in the southwestern province of Balochistan in mid-March.

Pakistani officials linked that hijacking to a continuation of the country’s worsening security environment, exacerbated by the ability of militants to cross the border to Afghanistan and subsequently return for future attacks. Pakistani officials have also claimed that militants have crept inside Pakistan under the garb of Afghan refugees to carry out terrorist attacks.

The plight of Afghan refugees has been worsened by reports that Donald Trump’s administration is likely to slow down — if not refuse — the issuance of U.S. visas to Afghans living in Pakistan. Many Afghans in Pakistan include those who assisted U.S. forces during their two decades in Afghanistan before the Americans withdrew in 2021.

Pakistan began hosting Afghan refugees in 1979 when the central Asian country was invaded by the former Soviet Union. In the almost five decades since, and in spite of the Soviet withdrawal of 1989, the flow of Afghans into Pakistan has continued.

This has been fueled by infighting between Afghan rivals and by the U.S. invasion after the 9/11 New York terrorist attacks, traced by Washington to militants on Afghan soil.

Afghan boys wave a flag as they head back with their families to Afghanistan from Pakistan on Nov. 10, 2023.   © Reuters

For Pakistan, the deadly legacy of militant attacks intensifying on its soil has added to the number of casualties across the country. According to data from last year compiled by the Islamabad based independent Centre for Research and Security Studies think tank, more than 2,500 civilians, security personnel and militants were killed in terrorist attacks in Pakistan in 2024, a 66% rise from 2023.

Many of the attacks in Pakistan, according to government officials, have been spearheaded by Taliban militants based in Afghanistan. According to a U.N. Security Council report in July 2024, there were at least an estimated 6,000 fighters from the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan [TTP] operating out of Afghanistan.

The TTP is a hardline militant group whose leaders are sworn enemies of Pakistan’s ruling structure. In carrying out attacks in Pakistan, it has used advanced weapons left behind by U.S.-led NATO forces that withdrew in 2021. The Taliban structure that took charge of Afghanistan four years ago has so far failed to curb the TTP attacks.

Afghanistan’s Taliban rulers remain globally isolated and internationally sanctioned, which raises questions over their ability to take charge of their country.

Controversial domestic policies such as banning girls from being educated at schools and forcing women to stay away from the workplace have placed the Taliban at sharp odds with foreign governments and vital multilateral institutions, including U.N. agencies.

Many of the Afghans now living in fear of being pushed out of Pakistan face the dangerous possibility of returning to the Taliban way of life as soon as they reenter Afghanistan.

Going forward, the international community can justifiably lobby for Pakistan to step back from large scale expulsions of Afghan nationals only by also helping it bolster its security framework and by assisting it economically. In the past, Pakistan’s leaders claimed to have begun work on fencing the country’s border with Afghanistan, though without success.

A step in the right direction would be supporting Pakistan’s reconnaissance of its porous border with Afghanistan. Improving Pakistan’s security apparatus by providing advanced helicopters could also support Islamabad in a meaningful way.

Such support can be provided while the West takes steps like providing Afghans stranded in Pakistan with opportunities to immigrate to secure destinations. It is already clear that forcing them to return to Afghanistan will only endanger the lives of many.

Short of such timely action, ignoring the plight of the Afghans caught in a terrible situation must not be an option. Afghanistan’s people have already paid a heavy price due to their country’s recurring conflict. That legacy of bloodshed must now finally come to an end.
item.author: Farhan Bokhari

item.title: Huawei’s automotive revenue up nearly sixfold despite U.S. clampdown
item.description:
Full-year net profit dips 28% amid ongoing 'future oriented' investments

TAIPEI — Huawei Technologies said on Monday its automotive business surged nearly sixfold in 2024, while its consumer business, including smartphones, rose more than 38% despite tighter U.S. export controls aimed at curbing China’s tech advancements.

Huawei, which the U.S. views as a security risk, reported revenue of 862.1 billion yuan ($118.16 billion) for 2024, up more than 22% from the previous year, and a net profit of 62.6 billion yuan, down 28% from 2023. Its revenue has now rebounded to a level similar to 2019, when the company was first added to the U.S. Entity List, a trade blacklist.

Revenue from all Huawei’s business groups grew in 2024, with the intelligent automotive solutions segment delivering the strongest gains at 26.4 billion yuan, a 474.4% increase from last year’s 4.7 billion yuan. While reiterating that it will not manufacture Huawei-branded cars itself, the company plans to continue providing integrated solutions, including smart control, self-driving capabilities and smart cockpit features, through partnerships with top Chinese automakers such as BYD, GAC Group and Dongfeng Motor.

Huawei said it shipped more than 23 million sets of intelligent automotive components in 2024, nearly seven times the 2023 level, and has helped its automaking partners build a total of 15 different models.

Revenue in its consumer electronics unit — which includes smartphones, the segment most severely affected by U.S. export controls — rose to 339 billion yuan in 2024. Huawei recently launched its high-end triple-fold smartphone overseas, in Malaysia, though most of its phone sales remain limited to China. Analysts do not expect a major upswing in shipments in 2025, as accessing sufficient mobile processors remains a challenge.

Meng Wanzhou, Huawei’s rotating chair, described the 2024 earnings as “in line” with expectations. She said the company will continue to strengthen its foundational ecosystems, including the Harmony operating system (OS) and its Kunpeng, Ascend and cloud computing platforms. Harmony OS is the company’s answer to Google Android. Kunpeng is intended to replace Intel and AMD offerings, while Ascend is an accelerated AI computing platform positioned as a China-made alternative to Nvidia’s products.

Huawei’s information, communication and technology infrastructure business, which includes its flagship telecom equipment business, grew 4.9% last year. Huawei Cloud reported a revenue increase of 8.5% while its digital power business, including solar tech-related solutions, advanced more than 24%. Huawei remains the global market leader in telecom infrastructure, followed by Ericsson, Nokia and Samsung.

Huawei did not provide details regarding its semiconductor development or supply chain management but said promoting “high quality” standards — particularly in its supply chain — will remain a key focus for 2025. A Nikkei Asia investigation found that Huawei continues to drive China’s tech, chip, electronics and equipment suppliers toward more competitive solutions. Semiconductor equipment maker SiCarrier has emerged as the latest example.

A Huawei spokesperson attributed the company’s net profit decline in 2024 to ongoing “future oriented” investments. Huawei’s research and development spending reached a record 179.7 billion yuan in 2024, equal to 20.8% of its total revenue. The company said it would continue to allocate more than 20% of its revenue to R&D in 2025.

Meanwhile, the U.S. has introduced multiple rounds of export controls to limit China’s access to foreign technologies. However, according to the U.S. think tank CSIS, Huawei has used shell companies to obtain significant quantities of AI chips from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. and has stockpiled large volumes of high-bandwidth memory, which is critical for AI computing.
